target_customer: Future buyers of platinum group metals and critical minerals; today paid by investors, with missions funded by venture capital
problem: Platinum group metals are scarce and expensive on Earth; the company aims to mine metal-rich asteroids and refine material in space at far lower mission cost than earlier attempts.
business_model: Asteroid mining and in-space refining of platinum group metals, sold on return (pre-revenue, venture funded)
product_category: Space resources and deep space spacecraft

founders.name: Matt Gialich
education: Master's in electrical engineering, Cal State Poly Pomona
founders.background_notes: Led flight software and GNC teams at Virgin Orbit; later Director of Vehicle Software at Bird (Pulse 2.0 interview, YC page).

founders.name: Jose Acain
education: Bachelor's in mathematics and Master's in mechatronics and robotics, Santa Clara University
founders.background_notes: Named as co-founder in the Pulse 2.0 interview and company about page; not listed on the YC page.

competitors.name: Planetary Resources
competitors.what: Earlier asteroid mining company backed by Larry Page and James Cameron
competitors.traction_then: Defunct by 2022; bought by ConsenSys in 2019 before reaching an asteroid
competitors.funding_then: Raised and spent tens of millions before sale

competitors.name: Deep Space Industries
competitors.what: Earlier asteroid mining firm targeting propellant and construction materials
competitors.traction_then: Sold to Bradford Space; never proved viability

technical_complexity.rationale: Requires low cost deep space spacecraft, autonomous operation and an unproven in-space refinery; the first refinery demo in 2023 could not be activated and the 2025 Odin probe lost communication.

defensibility.rationale: Hard hardware and a first commercial deep space license (2024) are barriers, but no proven revenue and few direct rivals.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No well resourced player pursued the same asteroid mining wedge; earlier entrants had collapsed.

market_need_then: Platinum group metals are rare on Earth and the founders argued cheaper launch (rideshare on SpaceX) made small deep space missions affordable for the first time, versus a roughly 450 million dollar mission cost cited for 2008 to 2010.

branding.domain_note: Moved from astroforge.io to astroforge.com (301 redirect observed 2026).

identity.visual_style: Bold lowercase tagline we mine asteroids, space themed
identity.voice_and_tone: Confident and mission driven; Mission Control language

branding.brand_signature: we mine asteroids tagline and the Roid Rage podcast
branding.community_and_virality: Gizmodo and Ars Technica coverage and a company podcast called Roid Rage; Norse mythology mission names (Brokkr, Odin, Vestri) are inferred from names only, no source states the theme.

brand_strength.rationale: Memorable subject and strong media coverage, but no sourced evidence of community, merchandise or the brand driving hiring or sales.

outcome_analysis: AstroForge raised about 13 million dollars of seed capital and a 40 million dollar Series A in August 2024 on the thesis that cheap rideshare launches make asteroid mining missions affordable. Its first 2023 refinery demonstration could not be activated and the Odin probe launched in February 2025 lost communication. The company remains active and was assembling its next vehicle in 2026, so the outcome is still open and technical risk remains the main issue.
notes: Seed amount of 13 million comes from Wikipedia and a Mercury article, which reports it as a round from Y Combinator and Initialized; exact date not stated. Series A cross-checked by Payload, Gizmodo, Aviation Week and the O'Melveny release; one tracker cites a Form D dated 2025-01-31. Founding date given as January 2022 by Wikipedia and as 2021 by CB Insights. Competitor source dates are approximate: the Mercury article was seen via search without a precise date, and both rivals were defunct or sold before the batch. Odin result per Wikipedia (communication failure).
